title: Hotkey surge paging runbook and mini-bench reports
summary: Investigation notes and small-run benchmarks to reproduce and mitigate tail-latency spikes caused by short-lived hotkey surges that trigger eviction -> paging cascades. Contains repro steps, measured telemetry, hypotheses, simple mitigations we tried, and recommended next experiments.
content:
Problem statement:
Observed intermittent p95/p99 tail latency spikes on multi-tenant GPU racks correlated with bursts of requests focused on small hot key sets. The pattern looks like: hotkey surge -> rapid resident-set churn -> eviction thrash -> device/host page activity -> token emission stalls and high p95. This doc collects lab reproductions, lightweight profiling artifacts, and short-term mitigations to try in canary.

Why this is different from previous KV notes: 
- Focus is on the transient 'surge' (seconds-long) behavior rather than steady-state steady hotset tuning.
- Includes a structured runbook to reproduce in a dev rack (steps we used) and short microbench scripts.
- Emphasis on cross-layer telemetry correlation (serving runtime eviction counters, OS pagefaults, memory-bandwidth traces) rather than only eviction heuristics.

Experiment setup (dev rack):
- HW: 1 x A100-80GB (dev) node, Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 11.8, runtime build from pr/4822 with extra eviction stats.
- Model: distilled-3B transformer, max-seq 1024, kv cache configured to keep 48GB on-device by default (slotting a small working set to trigger spillback when eviction occurs).
- Workload generator: synthetic_load.py (repo: serving-benchmarks), zipf distribution implementation. Command used: 
  python synthetic_load.py --qps 120 --duration 300 --zipf-alpha 1.2 --hotkey-fraction 0.02 --hotkey-count 50 --seq-mean 512 --burst-interval 45 --burst-factor 6
- Baselines: stable run with uniform access, then single-surge runs with warmup.

What we recorded:
- Runtime eviction metrics (per-second evict_rate, evict_bytes, reclaim_rate).
- OS: minor/major pagefaults via /proc/vmstat sampling, psutil pagefault counters, and eBPF trace for soft page faults on the host process.
- PCIe and NVLink transfer counters (nvtop/nvidia-smi sample), and GPU memory bw via nvprof sampling.
- System memory bandwidth using perf (uncore counters) to watch host-side saturation during spillback.
- Latency: end-to-end request latency histograms (p50/p90/p95/p99) and per-token emission stalls.

Key observations (summary):
1) Reproducible tail spikes tied to bursts: every configured burst (burst-factor 6 every 45s) produced a p95 jump from ~22ms to 150-420ms (variation across runs). p99 occasionally > 2s when combined with concurrent background occupancy churn from another tenant.
2) Eviction rate correlation: evict_rate increased ~8x during surge window; evictions were concentrated on large KV pages mapping to long-context sessions.
3) Paging activity: host minor pagefaults/sec rose 6-12x during the surge window. eBPF traces showed many of these are soft faults during GPU->host spillback and re-fetches when spilled entries were needed again within seconds.
4) Memory bandwidth: GPU HBM measured jumps up to ~1.1 TB/s sustained for short windows (peak) during rehydration; host-side DRAM bandwidth also spiked (observed via perf). The combined effect resulted in contention on the memory subsystem and queues in the runtime's IO threads.
5) Eviction churn pattern: the eviction TTL/aging heuristic we have tends to evict recently used but not-recently-accessed items when the hotkey distribution skew jumps transiently (because recency-decay is calibrated for longer timescales).
6) Prefetch/backfill thrash: the re-fetching mechanism attempts to prefetch multiple related KV pages leading to amplified I/O; during surge this multiplies the bandwidth demand because nearby pages are cold on device but hot in the request stream.

Hypotheses: 
- Short-lived hot surges cause the runtime to oscillate between evicting and reloading the same small set of keys because eviction cooldowns are too short and the prefetch strategy is too aggressive.
- Device<->host spillback implementation currently serializes too much work through a small number of IO threads, creating queueing latency when bandwidth demand spikes.
- The eviction heuristic's time-constant (decay) is tuned for minutes-scale workload shifts; for <10s surges it behaves suboptimally.

Microbench numbers (single representative run):
- Baseline (uniform) p95: 21ms, p99: 62ms, evict_rate: 120 pages/s.
- Surge window (as configured) p95: median 230ms (range 150-420ms), p99: 1.9s, evict_rate: 940 pages/s (7.8x).
- OS minor faults baseline: 14/s, surge: 95-170/s.
- GPU memory bw baseline: 400 GB/s, peak during surge: 1.05 TB/s (20s windows).
- IO thread queueing: avg queue length increased 5x; mean IO latency per spillback 38ms -> 220ms.

Short-term mitigations tried (and results):
1) Increase eviction cooldown window from 2s -> 12s (fast patch): reduced repeated re-eviction for the same keys; p95 improved by ~30% in isolated runs. Side effect: overall resident set used slightly more memory (about +6% RSS).
2) Cap prefetch parallelism to 2 pages at a time: lowered bandwidth amplification and reduced simultaneous IO queueing, p95 improved ~25%. But some throughput-sensitive long requests had slight increases in mean latency as prefetch can be useful for long sequence workloads.
3) IO thread pool increased from 2 -> 6: reduced single-thread queueing but raised overall host memory bandwidth contention; mixed results depending on host configuration.
4) Short-circuit policy: on detecting a hotkey surge (moving-window entropy drop below threshold) we temporarily switch to a 'pinned-hotset' mode: maintain an in-device pin list for top N keys for 12s. This is effective in synthetic runs (p95 back to ~35ms) but introduces complexity for eviction fairness.

Runbook: how to reproduce in dev (short):
1) checkout serving-benchmarks and serving-runtime with pr/4822 applied.
2) on dev A100 node: sudo ./scripts/setup-dev.sh; ensure nvml access.
3) start runtime with eviction telemetry enabled: RUNTIME_CONFIG=dev-hotkey.yaml ./bin/serve --enable-eviction-stats --eviction-cooldown=2
4) run generator: python synthetic_load.py --qps 120 --duration 300 --zipf-alpha 1.2 --hotkey-fraction 0.02 --hotkey-count 50 --burst-interval 45 --burst-factor 6 2>&1 | tee run1.log
5) collect traces: sudo ./scripts/collect-telemetry.sh --pid <runtime-pid> --out run1-trace.tar
6) post-process: python tools/telemetry-plot.py run1-trace.tar --metrics evict_rate,pagefaults,gpu_bw,latency

Suggested follow-ups (medium-term experiments):
- Adaptive cooldown: dynamic cooldown that grows when repeated re-eviction of the same keys is detected within a short window. Validate algorithm with different surge durations.
- Hotset pinning with eviction budget: maintain a small pinned list but charge pinned evictions against a budget to prevent starvation of other tenants. Evaluate fairness trade-offs in multi-tenant sims.
- Prefetch backpressure: add explicit backpressure channel so prefetch requests yield when IO queues exceed latency thresholds.
- Per-tenant bandwidth policing: explore throttling spillback for low-tier tenants during global memory-bandwidth spikes.
- IO batching improvements: merge small spillback requests into coalesced larger transfers to reduce per-request overhead under surge.

Data artifacts attached to this run (local filenames in /tmp artifacts):
- run1.log (request traces), run1-trace.tar (eviction+os+gpu telemetry), run1-postproc.csv (metrics by 1s bins).
- quick_plots/run1-evict-vs-latency.png, quick_plots/run1-gpu-bw.png

Open questions / things to be careful about:
- Pinned-hotset safety: how to surface to autoscaler/placement so we don't create ossified hot placements that reduce overall packability.
- Multi-tenant interactions: our synthetic runs show significant amplification when a second tenant has independent churn; need a multi-tenant stress harness.
- SLO design: what tail-latency thresholds are acceptable vs memory cost; exposes product questions for Dedicated/DH customers.

Immediate recommendation for canary:
- Deploy two short-term mitigations behind flags to a small canary fleet: eviction-cooldown=12s and prefetch-parallelism=2. Enable additional IO threads only if host bandwidth allows. Run with the surge generator for 24 hours across mixed-tenant sims and collect telemetry.

Next-owner / action items:
- Ava Chen: land lightweight flag + telemetry in pr/4822 and schedule canary run (WIP).
- Priya Nair: extend synthetic harness to run multi-tenant mixed-workloads (SERVE-2317).
- Diego Morales: prototype adaptive cooldown algorithm and baseline microbench (PR linked above).

Notes-to-self / rough TODOs:
- Add a simple 'hotkey surge detector' unit test to runtime (windowed entropy + max-accessor-count heuristic).
- Run the same tests on 2xA100 multi-GPU node to see if NVLink/PCIe offload changes the contention profile.
- Capture perf counters for PCIe NIC DMA if we move to multi-node reproduction.

References / links:
- internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4822
- ticket for longer-term: SERVE-2317
- benchmark harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-benchmarks/tree/main/synthetic_load

If you want to rerun a canned reproducer, ping me on Slack and I can share the run tarball (it’s ~430MB).
